A
Ad Library Audit
850 ads. Three testing layers. All live simultaneously.
Format variation on proven winners (same winning script, three different visual executions running at once). Offer tests on high-performing scripts (same creator, same script, discount vs. no discount as the only variable). And first-test launches on entirely new conditions like PCOS, hair loss, and male fatigue that weren't in their proven set yet. Proven angles get pushed to find their ceiling. New conditions get one shot before any resources are committed.
7 ads pulled from the library. These are the patterns I mapped.
B
Creative Angle Audit - 31 Ads
Every single ad they run uses the same angle type. Zero variety.
I tagged all 31 ads across four angle types. Every confirmed winner uses either a mechanism explanation ("why GLP-1 blocks digestion") or a convenience pitch ("replace 25 pills, eat it like a snack"). The chart below shows the full distribution and where the untouched white space is.
Angle Distribution Across All 31 Grüns Ads
How-To / Mechanism
84%
Expose / Callout
10%
Emotional
6%
Identity
0%
Across all 31 ads including every confirmed winner, not one creative has tried to make the customer feel like a different kind of person for taking Grüns. No "the woman who finally has her health handled." No athlete who doesn't cut corners. The identity angle is completely open. That's where I'd attack first.
C
Competitor Gap Analysis - AG1, Lemme, First Day - 9 Ads
Three gaps Grüns has never touched. All confirmed working for competitors.
Gap 1: The industry expose angle. AG1 wins with "no clinical trials, just generic ingredient research." First Day wins with "expensive urine / absorption block" framing. Grüns has zero ads like this despite having the perfect setup for it (pill fatigue condition already in their library).

Gap 2: Buyers who've already been burned by supplements. Every competitor runs at least one ad built for the skeptic. Grüns has none. As their ad spend scales, this audience grows. No creative for them means a ceiling on performance.

Gap 3: Women 40+ dealing with metabolic changes. Lemme owns this with two winners. Grüns hasn't touched it. Their GLP-1 female creative targets a different moment in the same woman's journey.

Step D

3 briefs built directly from the gaps above.

Brief 01
Pill Fatigue
Expose Angle Already tried supplements Static
Targets the woman who's been stacking supplements for a year and quietly suspects none of it absorbs. She spends $80-150/month. She knows what bioavailability means. She's a Stage 3 buyer. AG1 and First Day are winning with this exact psychology. Grüns has no creative for her despite pill fatigue being a proven condition in their library.
Contrarian Hook"I almost quit supplements entirely. Then I tried Grüns."
Listicle Hook"3 things every capsule brand doesn't tell you about absorption."
Brief 02
40+ Metabolic Slowdown
Identity Angle Knows she has a problem Static
Metabolic Mary, 42-55. Clean diet, exercises, labs say she's fine. Body changed after 40. She didn't have a dramatic breaking point. She just stopped recognizing herself. Lemme owns her with a practical pitch. Nobody has gone into the identity layer underneath where she's quietly missing the version of herself she used to be.
POV Hook"POV: You woke up feeling like yourself for the first time in three years."
If/Then Hook"Your body after 40 burns through nutrients faster than your diet replaces them."
Brief 03
GLP-1 Nutrient Depletion
Mechanism Angle 6+ months on GLP-1 UGC Video
Grüns' existing GLP-1 ads target the early user. This targets month 6 onward. She's depleted, energy is gone, doctor calls it a success. The mechanism is real: GLP-1 slows gastric motility, which reduces how much your gut absorbs. B vitamins, zinc, magnesium all drop. Nobody in Grüns' library explains this to the buyer who's already researching it.
Contrarian Hook"I almost stopped my GLP-1 because of what it was doing to my energy. Then I found Grüns."
Listicle Hook"3 things Grüns users on GLP-1 stop dealing with by week 2."

Step E

3 existing Grüns ads rewritten. Different angle each time.

Original
"I don't have time to take 25 pills anymore. Anymore."
How-To angle. Talks to someone still in the routine who finds it annoying.
Rewritten
"If you've stopped taking your supplements because the routine got embarrassing, this is for you."
Identity angle. Talks to the person who already quit.
The shift: The original wins on inconvenience. The rewrite targets identity collapse. Someone who wanted to be the person who takes care of their health and quietly stopped being that person. That's a different person in the audience who the original never reaches.
Original
"Nobody wants to talk about it, but half of you cannot poop regularly."
Expose angle. Makes you feel lied to by water, movement, probiotics.
Rewritten
"3 things your gut is telling you that you keep blaming on something else."
Emotional angle. Meets her in the quiet moment before she's ready to be challenged.
The shift: The original requires the viewer to accept a confrontational premise immediately. The rewrite leads with recognition. Bloating after normal meals. Low energy after a full night's sleep. Feeling heavy when the scale hasn't moved. When someone hears all three and thinks "that's me" they're already sold before the solution is mentioned.
Original
"What's the hardest part about bodybuilding? Eating your greens."
Convenience angle. Talks to someone who already knows greens are a problem.
Rewritten
"How is it possible that bodybuilders have the most disciplined diets in fitness and still are among the most micronutrient-deficient bodies on the planet?"
Identity angle. Targets the guy who thinks he's already covered.
The shift: The original targets someone who already knows greens are a gap. Gary at the beginning of this journey eats clean and thinks he's covered. This hook validates his identity as a disciplined athlete then drops a fact that breaks his belief. He asks why. That's the only way you reach someone who doesn't think they have a problem yet.
